sentences.text: The species I. peninsularensis is diagnosed by a nasal that reaches the 18th maxillary alveolus, the absence of an incisive foramen, oval external nares, and broad ornamented osteoderms.
All teeth are slender, conical, and possess curved crowns.
The trunk bears osteoderms that are wider than long, while the tail carries longer-than-wide subrectangular osteoderms, each with a front-to-back keel.
I. peninsularensis is the first confirmed freshwater-living thalattosuchian, contrasting with the marine habit of the type species.
Its bite force is among the strongest recorded for teleosaurs, rivaling that of derived machimosaurids.
The species lived in a low-energy lagoonal setting, offering rare insight into teleosaurid ecology.
Material for I. peninsularensis was collected at the Ban Nam Pun site in 2004.
Additional remains were uncovered at the Phu Noi locality in 2008, yielding ten specimens of varying ages.
The type locality for the species is the Khlong Min Formation in Thailand.
This contrasts with the freshwater habit of the type species.
The genus evolved convergent features with machimosaurids, such as robust jaws and strong muscle attachment sites.
Its lower jaw musculature provided a high posterior mechanical advantage, the greatest among known teleosaurs.
Researchers propose that the Phu Noi specimens may have gathered in water during a major drought, a behavior comparable to modern crocodilians.
An alternative view suggests the Phu Noi specimens died in a flash flood and were stranded as waters receded.
Indosinosuchus belongs to the family Teleosauridae.
Initial analyses placed it as a close relative of Machimosaurus hugii, but later work separated the two into distinct families, teleosaurids and machimosaurids.
Indosinosuchus lived during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous in present-day Thailand.
Specifically, I. peninsularensis ranges from the Bathonian to the Callovian, between 168.2 and 161.5 million years ago.
The precise age of Indosinosuchus remains contested, with vertebrate fossils indicating a Late Jurassic age and palynological evidence pointing to an Early Cretaceous age.
The validity of Indosinosuchus kalasinensis as a separate species was questioned in a 2026 study, which argued it may be synonymous with I. potamosiamensis.
Some researchers suggest that the lack of postcranial material for I. kalasinensis hampers clear phylogenetic placement.
Differences between I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis are debated as either reflecting distinct ecological niches or resulting from post-mortem skull distortion.
